title: Finite-size scaling of hetero-associative retrieval in continuous-signal-driven Ising spin systems
summary: Real-world physical signals are continuous and high-dimensional, yet the statistical-mechanics machinery of associative memory operates on discrete Ising spins. We bridge this divide through a multilayer Ising framework that couples a geometry-preserving continuous-to-Ising encoder (PCA whitening composed with SimHash random-hyperplane projection) to Kanter-Sompolinsky pseudo-inverse memory couplings, embedded directly into the local-field equations of a tri-layer hetero-associative system. The pseudo-inverse correction renders the equal-weight mixture state thermodynamically unstable, so that thermal fluctuations break the cross-modal symmetry and select a single global winner. We further establish a dynamical duality: parallel (Little) updates are structurally required to ignite the cross-modal signal avalanche from a single cued layer, whereas sequential (Glauber) sweeps resolve symmetric superpositions. The operational storage capacity obeys the Amit-Gutfreund-Sompolinsky finite-size correction $α_c(N)=α_c(\infty)-c\,N^{-1/2}$, extrapolating to an asymptotic operational limit $α_c(\infty)\approx 0.50$ under macroscopic-basin retrieval. Applied to multi-channel sleep polysomnography (PhysioNet Sleep-EDF), the architecture reconstructs the macroscopic sleep state on parietal EEG and EOG axes from a single noisy frontal-EEG cue, demonstrating cross-modal recall in the presence of quenched biological disorder.

AI.tldr: The paper bridges continuous physical signals to discrete Ising spin associative memory via a multilayer framework (PCA whitening + SimHash projection + pseudo-inverse couplings), establishing dynamical duality between parallel and sequential updates, achieving asymptotic storage capacity α_c(∞)≈0.50, and demonstrating cross-modal sleep state reconstruction from noisy EEG cues on PhysioNet Sleep-EDF data.
AI.motivation: Real-world physical signals are continuous and high-dimensional, yet existing associative memory models operate on discrete Ising spins, creating a fundamental representational gap that limits applicability to real sensory data.
AI.method: A multilayer Ising framework coupling a geometry-preserving continuous-to-Ising encoder (PCA whitening + SimHash random-hyperplane projection) with Kanter-Sompolinsky pseudo-inverse memory couplings, embedded in tri-layer hetero-associative local-field equations, analyzed under parallel (Little) and sequential (Glauber) update dynamics.
AI.result: Pseudo-inverse correction renders the equal-weight mixture state thermodynamically unstable, enabling thermal symmetry breaking. Parallel updates ignite cross-modal signal avalanche; sequential updates resolve symmetric superpositions. Storage capacity follows α_c(N)=α_c(∞)-c N^{-1/2} with asymptotic limit α_c(∞)≈0.50. Applied to sleep-EDF data, architecture reconstructs sleep states from single noisy frontal-EEG cue.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework successfully bridges continuous physical signals and discrete associative memory, achieving cross-modal recall under quenched biological disorder with theoretically characterized finite-size scaling of storage capacity.

title: Quantum Criticality in Monolayer Amorphous Carbon
summary: Amorphous solids represent the extreme limit of broken translational symmetry, in which the absence of long-range order removes well-defined crystal momenta and invalidates the Bloch description of electronic states. Monolayer amorphous carbon (MAC) has emerged as a unique realization of a strictly two-dimensional (2D) amorphous lattice defined by a structurally contiguous but topologically disordered $sp^2$-bonded random network devoid of any defined long-range crystal symmetry. From atomic-resolution measurements of multifractal wavefunctions, we show that disorder in MAC effectively localizes the low-energy part of the electronic spectrum but retains an extended critical-like state near the band centre ($E\sim 0$). We conjecture that this state is protected from topological disorder by remnant chiral symmetry surviving within the continuous random network, described by a Wess-Zumino-Witten (WZW) topological term. Near criticality, we verify the multifractal scaling relation $η= -Δ_2$, providing quantitative agreement between independently measured spatial correlation decay and multifractal scaling exponents. Our results are confirmed by atomistic tight-binding calculations that closely mirror the multifractal scaling near $E\sim 0$. Our results establish MAC as the first strictly 2D amorphous electronic system to exhibit Anderson criticality driven purely by topological disorder

AI.tldr: Monolayer amorphous carbon (MAC) exhibits Anderson criticality with a critical-like state near the band center protected by remnant chiral symmetry, verified through multifractal scaling measurements and tight-binding calculations.
AI.motivation: To investigate electronic states in a strictly 2D amorphous system (MAC) where topological disorder replaces crystalline symmetry, exploring whether Anderson criticality can emerge purely from structural disorder without long-range order.
AI.method: Atomic-resolution multifractal wavefunction measurements, multifractal scaling relation η = -Δ₂ verification, atomistic tight-binding calculations, and Wess-Zumino-Witten (WZW) topological term analysis.
AI.result: Disorder in MAC localizes low-energy electronic states but preserves an extended critical-like state near E∼0; multifractal scaling exponents from spatial correlation decay and multifractal scaling agree quantitatively; tight-binding calculations confirm the multifractal scaling near E∼0.
AI.conclusion: MAC is the first strictly 2D amorphous electronic system exhibiting Anderson criticality driven purely by topological disorder, with chiral symmetry protecting the critical state.

title: FKPP fronts in quenched random media
summary: We study numerically the evolution of one-dimensional FKPP fronts initiated from steep initial conditions in the presence of a quenched random growth rate. Compared to both the homogeneous case (with velocity $v_0$) and deterministic disorder, quenched randomness increases the average propagation speed. We show that the velocity shift relative to the homogeneous case scales linearly with the disorder variance $σ^2$, with a universal prefactor -- independent of the specific distribution of the disorder -- such that $v = v_0 + a σ^2$, with $a \approx 0.02432 \pm 0.00002$. Moreover, the front position exhibits diffusive fluctuations across disorder realizations. The corresponding effective diffusion coefficient scales quadratically with $σ$, $D = \frac{b^2 σ^2}{2}$, with $b \approx 0.223 \pm 0.002$. These results suggest a universal statistical response of FKPP fronts to quenched heterogeneity.

AI.tldr: This numerically studied paper investigates how quenched random growth rates affect one-dimensional FKPP fronts. It finds that quenched randomness increases propagation speed relative to the homogeneous case, with a velocity shift scaling linearly with disorder variance (universal prefactor ~0.02432), and the front position shows diffusive fluctuations with an effective diffusion coefficient scaling quadratically with disorder strength.
AI.motivation: To understand how quenched (static) random heterogeneity in growth rates influences the propagation dynamics of FKPP fronts, beyond the well-studied homogeneous and deterministic disorder cases.
AI.method: Numerical simulation of 1D FKPP fronts with steep initial conditions, incorporating a quenched random growth rate. The disorder variance σ² is varied, and the front velocity and position fluctuations are measured across disorder realizations.
AI.result: The velocity shift relative to the homogeneous case scales as v = v₀ + aσ² with a ≈ 0.02432, and the effective diffusion coefficient of front position fluctuations scales as D = b²σ²/2 with b ≈ 0.223. Both prefactors are universal and independent of the specific disorder distribution.
AI.conclusion: Quenched disorder accelerates FKPP fronts in a universal manner, with well-defined scaling laws for both the velocity shift and the diffusive fluctuations, suggesting a universal statistical response to quenched heterogeneity.

title: From Chaos to Synchrony in Recurrent Excitatory-Inhibitory Networks with Target-Specific Inhibition
comment: Supplemental Material is added as an additional PDF file at the end of the main text
summary: Biological neural networks can operate in qualitatively distinct dynamical regimes, and transitions between these regimes are thought to underlie changes in computation and behavior. The seminal work of Sompolinsky, Crisanti, and Sommers (SCS) showed that random recurrent networks undergo a transition from quiescence to asynchronous chaos, establishing a paradigmatic link between random connectivity, dynamical instability, and internally generated fluctuations in neural circuits. Here, we extend this framework to two-population firing-rate networks with segregated excitatory and inhibitory neurons and target-specific inhibitory couplings that break excitation--inhibition balance. Using dynamical mean-field theory, we derive self-consistent equations for the macroscopic mean activities and autocorrelations, together with stability criteria distinguishing mean-driven and fluctuation-driven instabilities. We show that target-specific inhibition organizes the phase diagram into three qualitative classes: inhibition-dominated or strictly balanced networks display only quiescent activity and asynchronous chaos; excitation-dominated networks display persistent activity together with either synchronous chaos with non-vanishing mean activity or coherent oscillations, depending on the stability-matrix eigenvalues. Crucially, coherent oscillations do not coexist with chaotic fluctuations around the periodic mean trajectory; rather, their onset suppresses the chaotic component, reminiscent of input-induced suppression of chaos. These results generalize SCS theory to recurrent networks with explicit excitatory--inhibitory structure and identify target-specific inhibition as a key control parameter for large-scale neural dynamics.

AI.tldr: This paper extends Sompolinsky, Crisanti, and Sommers (SCS) theory to two-population firing-rate networks with segregated excitatory and inhibitory neurons and target-specific inhibitory couplings, revealing three dynamical regimes: inhibition-dominated networks show only quiescence or asynchronous chaos; excitation-dominated networks show persistent activity with synchronous chaos or coherent oscillations, where oscillations suppress chaos.
AI.motivation: To extend the classical SCS framework of random recurrent networks to more biologically realistic networks with explicit excitatory-inhibitory structure and target-specific inhibition, and to understand how these structural features shape the dynamical phase diagram.
AI.method: Dynamical mean-field theory to derive self-consistent equations for macroscopic mean activities and autocorrelations, along with stability criteria distinguishing mean-driven and fluctuation-driven instabilities.
AI.result: Target-specific inhibition organizes the phase diagram into three classes: inhibition-dominated/balanced networks (quiescence or asynchronous chaos), excitation-dominated networks (persistent activity with synchronous chaos or coherent oscillations). Coherent oscillations suppress chaotic fluctuations rather than coexisting with them.
AI.conclusion: Target-specific inhibition serves as a key control parameter for large-scale neural dynamics, and the onset of oscillations suppresses chaos, analogous to input-induced suppression of chaos.

title: A QPINN Framework with Quantum Trainable Embeddings for the Lid-Driven Cavity Problem
summary: The steady incompressible Navier--Stokes equations pose significant computational challenges due to their nonlinear convective terms and pressure--velocity coupling. Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) provide a mesh-free framework for approximating such systems, but classical PINNs can experience optimization difficulties in nonlinear flow regimes. In this work, we propose a quantum physics-informed neural network (QPINN) framework with a quantum neural network (QNN)-based trainable embedding for the lid-driven cavity problem. The proposed approach uses a QNN to learn data-adaptive quantum feature maps that encode spatial coordinates before they are processed by a variational quantum circuit within a physics-informed loss formulation. Numerical experiments show that the proposed QNN-TE-QPINN exhibits stable training behavior and competitive solution accuracy compared with classical PINNs and hybrid quantum models using classical embeddings, while requiring significantly fewer trainable parameters. Rather than claiming computational speedup, these results highlight the potential of trainable quantum embeddings for parameter-efficient physics-informed learning. The findings suggest that embedding design plays an important role in quantum-assisted PDE solvers and support further investigation of QNN-based trainable embeddings for nonlinear fluid dynamics benchmarks.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a quantum physics-informed neural network (QPINN) with a trainable quantum embedding (QNN-TE-QPINN) for solving the lid-driven cavity flow problem. The approach uses a quantum neural network to learn adaptive feature maps within a physics-informed loss formulation, achieving stable training and competitive accuracy with fewer parameters compared to classical PINNs and hybrid quantum models.
AI.motivation: Classical PINNs face optimization difficulties in nonlinear flow regimes (e.g., Navier-Stokes equations), and existing quantum models lack trainable embedding mechanisms for PDE solving.
AI.method: Proposes a QPINN framework where a QNN learns data-adaptive quantum feature maps to encode spatial coordinates, processed by a variational quantum circuit under a physics-informed loss formulation.
AI.result: QNN-TE-QPINN achieves stable training behavior and competitive solution accuracy compared to classical PINNs and hybrid quantum models using classical embeddings, while using significantly fewer trainable parameters.
AI.conclusion: Trainable quantum embeddings are effective for parameter-efficient physics-informed learning, and embedding design is important for quantum-assisted PDE solvers, warranting further investigation for nonlinear fluid dynamics benchmarks.

title: Universal Spin Squeezing Dynamical Phase Transitions across Lattice Geometries, Dimensions, and Microscopic Couplings
summary: Recent work has identified a dynamical squeezing phase transition in power-law interacting bilayer XXZ spin models, separating a fully collective phase with Heisenberg-limited squeezing from a partially-collective phase with universal critical scaling. Here we test and establish the universality of this transition along two qualitatively different microscopic axes: lattice geometry, by studying square, triangular, and honeycomb $2\mathrm{D}$ bilayers as well as $1\mathrm{D}$ ladders, and a symmetry-preserving rescaling $λ$ of the interlayer couplings relative to the intralayer ones. Combining a Bogoliubov instability analysis with discrete truncated Wigner simulations, we find that the transition persists across all four lattice geometries and over a wide range of $λ$ with critical exponents consistent within error, providing strong evidence for a genuine non-equilibrium universality class. The Bogoliubov theory recovers the previously identified scaling $a_Z^* \propto L$ in the long-range interacting regime $α< d+2$, and yields an analytical scaling $a_Z^* \propto L^{2/(α-d)}$ for the critical aspect ratio with system size for $α>d+2$, with $α$ the power-law exponent in dimension $d$. This uncovers a previously unrecognized sub-linear regime for short-range interactions. By tuning $λ$ we vary the interlayer coupling strength at fixed layer spacing, demonstrating that the dynamical transition can be driven purely through interaction engineering without modifying the underlying geometry. These findings provide a versatile route toward controlling entanglement generation in Rydberg-array, polar molecule, and trapped-ion platforms with applications in quantum sensing and simulation.

AI.tldr: This paper tests and confirms the universality of a dynamical squeezing phase transition in power-law interacting bilayer XXZ spin models across different lattice geometries (square, triangular, honeycomb 2D bilayers and 1D ladders) and interlayer coupling strengths, identifying a genuine non-equilibrium universality class with consistent critical exponents. The study reveals new analytical scaling for the critical aspect ratio and demonstrates that the transition can be engineered purely through interaction tuning.
AI.motivation: To test and establish the universality of a previously identified dynamical squeezing phase transition in power-law interacting bilayer XXZ spin models by examining its robustness across different lattice geometries and interlayer coupling strengths, thereby determining whether it constitutes a genuine non-equilibrium universality class.
AI.method: Combined Bogoliubov instability analysis with discrete truncated Wigner simulations, studying square, triangular, honeycomb 2D bilayers and 1D ladders, and varying a symmetry-preserving rescaling λ of interlayer couplings relative to intralayer ones.
AI.result: The transition persists across all four lattice geometries and over a wide range of λ with consistent critical exponents. Bogoliubov theory recovers scaling a_Z^* ∝ L for α < d+2 and yields new analytical scaling a_Z^* ∝ L^{2/(α-d)} for α > d+2, revealing a previously unrecognized sub-linear regime for short-range interactions.
AI.conclusion: The dynamical squeezing phase transition constitutes a genuine non-equilibrium universality class. It can be driven purely through interaction engineering without modifying geometry, providing a versatile route for controlling entanglement generation in quantum platforms such as Rydberg arrays, polar molecules, and trapped ions, with applications in quantum sensing and simulation.

title: All-Electric Quantum State Transfer via Spin-Orbit Phase Matching
summary: Semiconductor hole-spin qubits offer a promising route to quantum computation due to their weak hyperfine interaction, and strong intrinsic spin-orbit coupling enabling electric control of qubits. Scalable architectures, however, require coherent long-distance quantum state transfer, which is hindered in these systems by spin-orbit induced anisotropic exchange. Here we show that this limitation can be overcome by using an all-electric control protocol. By tuning the electric field strength, we identify discrete spin-orbit phase-matching conditions that restore near-perfect state transfer, independent of the rotation axis. Complementarily, controlling the electric field direction aligns the spin-orbit axis, suppressing excitation non-conserving processes and enabling robust transfer without fine tuning. Our results establish that electrical control of spin-orbit phases through either magnitude tuning or axis alignment as a practical route for robust quantum information transport in hole-spin quantum dot arrays.

AI.tldr: Hole-spin qubits can achieve coherent long-distance quantum state transfer via all-electric control that tunes spin-orbit phase-matching conditions or aligns the spin-orbit axis, overcoming the limitation of anisotropic exchange.
AI.motivation: Scalable quantum computing with hole-spin qubits requires coherent long-distance quantum state transfer, which is hindered by spin-orbit induced anisotropic exchange.
AI.method: All-electric control protocol: (1) tuning electric field strength to identify discrete spin-orbit phase-matching conditions, and (2) controlling electric field direction to align the spin-orbit axis.
AI.result: Near-perfect state transfer restored independent of rotation axis via phase-matching; robust transfer achieved without fine tuning via axis alignment.
AI.conclusion: Electrical control of spin-orbit phases—through magnitude tuning or axis alignment—offers a practical route for robust quantum information transport in hole-spin quantum dot arrays.

title: Winning Lottery Tickets in Neural Networks via a Quantum-Inspired Classical Algorithm
summary: Quantum machine learning (QML) aims to accelerate machine learning tasks by exploiting quantum computation. Previous work studied a QML algorithm for selecting sparse subnetworks from large shallow neural networks. Instead of directly solving an optimization problem over a large-scale network, this algorithm constructs a sparse subnetwork by sampling hidden nodes from an optimized probability distribution defined using the ridgelet transform. The quantum algorithm performs this sampling in time $O(D)$ in the data dimension $D$, whereas a naive classical implementation relies on handling exponentially many candidate nodes and hence takes $\exp[O(D)]$ time. In this work, we construct and analyze a quantum-inspired fully classical algorithm for the same sampling task. We show that our algorithm runs in time $O(\operatorname{poly}(D))$, thereby removing the exponential dependence on $D$ from the previous classical approach. Numerical simulations show that the proposed sampler achieves empirical risk comparable to exact sampling from the optimized distribution and substantially lower than sampling from the non-optimized uniform distribution, while also exhibiting exponentially improved runtime scaling compared with the conventional classical implementation. These successful dequantization results show that sparse subnetwork selection via optimized sampling can be achieved classically with polynomial data-dimension scaling on conventional computers without quantum hardware, providing an alternative to the existing quantum algorithm.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a classical (quantum-inspired) algorithm for selecting sparse subnetworks from large shallow neural networks via optimized sampling, achieving O(poly(D)) runtime in data dimension D, removing the exponential dependence of naive classical approaches, and matching the performance of a previously proposed quantum algorithm.
AI.motivation: Previous work proposed a quantum algorithm for sparse subnetwork selection that runs in O(D) time, while a naive classical implementation takes exp[O(D)] time due to handling exponentially many candidate nodes. The authors aim to determine whether this quantum advantage is fundamental or can be dequantized.
AI.method: The authors construct a quantum-inspired fully classical algorithm for sampling hidden nodes from an optimized probability distribution defined via the ridgelet transform. They analyze its runtime complexity and validate it with numerical simulations comparing empirical risk against exact optimized sampling and uniform sampling.
AI.result: The classical algorithm runs in O(poly(D)) time, eliminating the exponential dependence on D. Numerical simulations show comparable empirical risk to exact optimized sampling, substantially lower risk than uniform sampling, and exponentially improved runtime scaling versus the naive classical implementation.
AI.conclusion: Sparse subnetwork selection via optimized sampling can be achieved classically with polynomial data-dimension scaling, providing a dequantized alternative to the quantum algorithm and demonstrating that the quantum advantage is not fundamental for this task.

title: From Hilbert's Tenth Problem to Quantum Speedup: Explicit Oracles for Bounded Diophantine Systems
summary: Solving non-linear Diophantine systems lies at the mathematical core of integer optimization and cryptography. While the general unbounded problem is undecidable, even over bounded integer domains it remains classically intractable in the worst case. In this work, we introduce a fully reversible quantum algorithmic framework tailored to solve arbitrary polynomial Diophantine equations over bounded integer domains. The core of our approach is the explicit, gate-level synthesis of an evaluation oracle for amplitude amplification. By coherently evaluating polynomial constraints via in-place two's complement arithmetic and routing operations into a single recycled accumulator, this garbage-free strategy achieves a compact and scalable synthesis of the underlying non-linear arithmetic. Through analytical derivations and empirical circuit simulations, we prove that the overall spatial complexity is bounded by $q = \mathcal{O}((n + d^2)\log_2 N)$ logical qubits for $n$ variables, maximum degree $d$, and interval length $N$. The non-Clifford Toffoli depth is upper-bounded by $\mathcal{O}(q^2)$. This structural scaling exponent remains invariant to the variable count, modulated linearly only by the coefficients' Hamming weights. By moving beyond abstract black-box assumptions, this explicit architectural synthesis guarantees that the necessary quantum arithmetic acts as a bounded polynomial overhead. This ensures a quadratic speedup over classical exhaustive search, whether retrieving a unique assignment or dynamically enumerating an unknown number of solutions.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a fully reversible quantum algorithmic framework for solving arbitrary polynomial Diophantine equations over bounded integer domains, with explicit gate-level synthesis of an evaluation oracle for amplitude amplification, achieving bounded polynomial quantum overhead and a quadratic speedup over classical exhaustive search.
AI.motivation: Solving non-linear Diophantine systems is fundamental to integer optimization and cryptography, yet remains classically intractable even over bounded domains. The authors aim to develop a quantum approach that provides provable speedup while moving beyond abstract black-box assumptions about the oracle.
AI.method: The approach uses a fully reversible quantum algorithmic framework with explicit gate-level synthesis of an evaluation oracle for amplitude amplification. It employs in-place two's complement arithmetic and routing operations into a single recycled accumulator to achieve garbage-free, compact synthesis of non-linear arithmetic.
AI.result: Spatial complexity is bounded by q = O((n + d²) log₂ N) logical qubits for n variables, maximum degree d, and interval length N. Non-Clifford Toffoli depth is upper-bounded by O(q²). The scaling exponent is invariant to variable count and linearly modulated by coefficients' Hamming weights.
AI.conclusion: The explicit architectural synthesis guarantees bounded polynomial quantum overhead, ensuring a quadratic speedup over classical exhaustive search for both retrieving unique assignments and dynamically enumerating unknown numbers of solutions.

title: Graphical Algebraic Geometry: From Ideals and Varieties to Quantum Calculi
summary: We introduce Graphical Algebraic Geometry (GAG), a family of diagrammatic languages extending the Graphical Linear Algebra programme. We construct several languages within this family and prove that they are universal and complete for the corresponding (co)span semantics of commutative algebras and affine varieties. This framework provides clear graphical representations of algebraic structures -- such as polynomials, ideals, and varieties -- enabling intuitive yet rigorous diagrammatic reasoning. We showcase two practical viewpoints on GAG. First, we show that instances of counting constraint satisfaction problem (#CSP) are recast as rewrite problems of closed diagrams in GAG. This means that deciding rewritability in GAG is #P-hard, and GAG can be viewed as a complete and compositional rewrite system for networks of polynomial constraints. Second, we characterize the qudit ZH calculus, a diagrammatic language for quantum computation, as an extension of Graphical Algebraic Geometry. This establishes the correspondence that Graphical Algebraic Geometry is to the ZH calculus what Graphical Linear Algebra is to the ZX calculus. Using this construction, we show that computing amplitudes in qudit ZH requires only a constant number of queries to a GAG oracle.

AI.tldr: GAG is a family of diagrammatic languages extending Graphical Linear Algebra, proven universal and complete for (co)span semantics of commutative algebras and affine varieties, with applications to #CSP (rewritability is #P-hard) and qudit ZH calculus as an extension.
AI.motivation: To provide a graphical, intuitive yet rigorous framework for representing algebraic structures (polynomials, ideals, varieties) by extending the Graphical Linear Algebra programme.
AI.method: Construct multiple languages within the GAG family and prove universal completeness for (co)span semantics of commutative algebras and affine varieties. Show #CSP instances as rewrite problems of closed diagrams, and characterize qudit ZH calculus as an extension of GAG.
AI.result: Deciding rewritability in GAG is #P-hard; GAG serves as a complete and compositional rewrite system for polynomial constraint networks. Qudit ZH amplitudes require only a constant number of queries to a GAG oracle.
AI.conclusion: GAG bridges algebraic geometry and diagrammatic reasoning, with implications for constraint satisfaction complexity and quantum computation via the ZH calculus.

title: QUACOD: Quantum Optimization via Coordinate Descent for Scalable Drone Scheduling
summary: Quantum computing has demonstrated its potential to solve various optimization problems, including drone scheduling, which is important not only for drone delivery but also for logistics in general. However, one of the main obstacles is that practical drone scheduling settings typically require quantum resources that current hardware cannot provide. Therefore, in this work, we introduce a new Quantum Optimization via Coordinate Descent (QUACOD) approach to address this problem under the constraint of a limited number of available qubits. By leveraging coordinate descent, QUACOD decomposes the original high-complexity problem into multiple subproblems, which are then solved using quantum optimization. In our experiments, QUACOD outperforms the state-of-the-art (SOTA) quantum-based drone scheduling method not only in optimized drone completion times but also in scalability, handling up to 5 times more drones and 35 times more routes. In addition, QUACOD demonstrates that hardware-efficient circuits are effective for optimization problems. Together, these contributions advance quantum computing toward practical applications in the noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) era.

AI.tldr: QUACOD is a quantum-classical hybrid algorithm using coordinate descent to decompose large drone scheduling problems into smaller subproblems solvable on limited qubit hardware, outperforming SOTA methods by handling 5x more drones and 35x more routes while improving completion times.
AI.motivation: Practical drone scheduling requires quantum resources beyond current NISQ hardware capabilities; existing quantum methods cannot scale to real-world problem sizes due to qubit limitations.
AI.method: Coordinate descent decomposes the original high-complexity optimization problem into multiple smaller subproblems, each solvable via quantum optimization on limited qubits, using hardware-efficient circuits.
AI.result: QUACOD outperforms SOTA quantum drone scheduling in completion times and scalability, handling up to 5x more drones and 35x more routes.
AI.conclusion: Hardware-efficient circuits are effective for optimization; QUACOD advances quantum computing toward practical NISQ-era applications in logistics.

title: C-Phase-Aware Compilation for Efficient Fault-Tolerant Quantum Execution
summary:
Achieving practical quantum advantage on fault-tolerant quantum computers (FTQC) is fundamentally constrained by the substantial spatial and temporal overheads required to map logical operations onto physical hardware. Existing compilation approaches typically adopt coarse-grained, slice-based abstractions that overlook fine-grained microarchitectural effects, such as routing contention, leading to inefficient resource utilization and limited alignment between algorithm structure and hardware capabilities.
  This work presents a microarchitecture-aware compilation approach that integrates algorithmic structure directly with lattice surgery (LS) execution. By leveraging the commutativity of C-Phase operations, the method transforms inherently sequential gate sequences into concurrent multi-target interactions, effectively removing artificial dependencies and exposing significant instruction-level parallelism. To enable this, we design a dynamic, event-driven scheduling strategy that accurately models spatial layout and routing constraints, allowing operations to overlap in time while minimizing contention. Through improved coordination of computation and communication, this approach substantially reduces idle resources and achieves up to a 59.7$\times$ reduction in execution time compared to standard baselines.

AI.tldr: A microarchitecture-aware compilation method for fault-tolerant quantum computers that leverages commutativity of C-Phase operations to transform sequential gates into concurrent multi-target interactions, using dynamic event-driven scheduling to reduce execution time by up to 59.7× over standard baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing FTQC compilation approaches use coarse-grained, slice-based abstractions that ignore fine-grained microarchitectural effects like routing contention, leading to inefficient resource utilization and poor alignment between algorithm structure and hardware capabilities. This work aims to bridge this gap by integrating algorithmic structure with lattice surgery execution.
AI.method: The approach leverages commutativity of C-Phase operations to transform sequential gate sequences into concurrent multi-target interactions, removing artificial dependencies and exposing instruction-level parallelism. A dynamic, event-driven scheduling strategy is designed that models spatial layout and routing constraints, enabling overlapping operations while minimizing contention.
AI.result: The approach achieves up to a 59.7× reduction in execution time compared to standard baselines by substantially reducing idle resources through improved coordination of computation and communication.
AI.conclusion: Microarchitecture-aware compilation that integrates algorithmic structure with lattice surgery execution can dramatically improve FTQC efficiency by exposing instruction-level parallelism and reducing contention, offering a pathway toward practical quantum advantage.

title: Transitions as the Native Objects of Dispersive Light-Matter Dynamics
summary: We introduce a framework where light-matter transitions, rather than states, are the primary dynamical objects. Successive compositions of elementary transitions yield multiphoton processes with compact diagrammatic bookkeeping of resonant and off-resonant pathways. This approach enables transparent derivations of effective high-order Hamiltonians in the dispersive regime, foundational to quantum-information applications. Applied to the paradigmatic Jaynes-Cummings model, our framework reveals a photon-number-independent intrinsic Rabi frequency and persistent polaritonic hybridization in the dispersive regime, unifying resonant and dispersive limits.

AI.tldr: Introduces a framework where light-matter transitions are the primary dynamical objects, enabling transparent derivations of effective high-order Hamiltonians and revealing unified descriptions of resonant and dispersive regimes in the Jaynes-Cummings model.
AI.motivation: To develop a framework that treats light-matter transitions as fundamental objects, enabling simpler derivations of effective Hamiltonians in the dispersive regime and unifying resonant and dispersive limits in quantum optics.
AI.method: The framework uses successive compositions of elementary transitions with diagrammatic bookkeeping to handle multiphoton processes, applied to the Jaynes-Cummings model to analyze resonant and off-resonant pathways.
AI.result: Reveals a photon-number-independent intrinsic Rabi frequency and persistent polaritonic hybridization in the dispersive regime, unifying the resonant and dispersive limits.
AI.conclusion: The transition-based framework provides a compact and transparent approach for deriving effective high-order Hamiltonians, with potential applications in quantum information processing.

title: Effective Hamiltonians in Cavity and Waveguide QED from Transition-Operator Diagrammatic Perturbation Theory
summary: We propose an adiabatic-elimination formalism in the dispersive regime based on a transition-centric perturbation theory. The perturbative expansion is recast into a diagrammatic framework, while adiabatic elimination is implemented through controlled projections onto transition subspaces. Our approach applies systematically at arbitrary perturbation order, and is suited to multilevel systems and multiple qubits in both cavity and waveguide quantum electrodynamics. It ultimately enables the explicit construction of effective higher-order Hamiltonians while bypassing important limitations of existing techniques, thereby providing a practical toolbox for multiphoton processes in the dispersive regime.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a new adiabatic-elimination formalism using transition-centric perturbation theory and diagrammatic methods to systematically construct effective higher-order Hamiltonians for multiphoton processes in dispersive regime quantum electrodynamics.
AI.motivation: Existing techniques for adiabatic elimination in the dispersive regime have important limitations, particularly when applied to multilevel systems, multiple qubits, or higher-order multiphoton processes. A more systematic and general framework is needed.
AI.method: The method recasts perturbative expansion into a diagrammatic framework and implements adiabatic elimination through controlled projections onto transition subspaces, based on a transition-centric perturbation theory. It applies systematically at arbitrary perturbation order.
AI.result: The approach enables explicit construction of effective higher-order Hamiltonians while bypassing limitations of existing techniques, and is suited to multilevel systems and multiple qubits in both cavity and waveguide quantum electrodynamics.
AI.conclusion: The formalism provides a practical toolbox for analyzing multiphoton processes in the dispersive regime, applicable to a wide range of quantum electrodynamic systems at arbitrary perturbation order.

title: Decoherence in matter-wave Talbot interference: a hydrodynamic probability-flow analysis
summary: We investigate the suppression of matter-wave Talbot interference under environmentally induced decoherence. The system is modeled as an atomic beam diffracted by a periodic grating, whose transverse dynamics is described within the paraxial approximation. Environmental coupling is introduced through an effective open-system model that exponentially damps spatial coherences between diffracted components, allowing a continuous interpolation between the coherent Talbot regime and the incoherent far-field diffraction limit. Besides the usual intensity and transverse-momentum distributions, we analyze the local probability flow associated with the diffracted matter wave. The corresponding Bohmian, or hydrodynamic, representation is used here as a diagnostic tool fully equivalent to the standard quantum description, with no additional assumptions beyond the probability current of the paraxial wave field. In the present Talbot geometry, this analysis shows how decoherence progressively suppresses the carpet structure and smooths the transverse-momentum distribution, while the flow may remain organized into channels determined by the grating periodicity. The results illustrate, in a periodic matter-wave Talbot geometry, that the loss of visible interference and the loss of dynamical pathway separation need not occur simultaneously. In particular, flux-channel structures can persist in parameter regimes where multi-slit interference features have already been strongly reduced. This distinction provides a local characterization of decoherence in matter-wave Talbot interferometry and complements previous trajectory-based analyses of coherence loss in simpler interference and confined geometries.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how decoherence suppresses matter-wave Talbot interference, showing that while interference fringes and momentum distributions smooth out, the underlying probability flow can remain organized into periodic channels even when visible interference is lost.
AI.motivation: To understand the distinct roles of decoherence on interference visibility versus dynamical flow structures in periodic matter-wave systems, using the Talbot effect as a testbed.
AI.method: The authors model an atomic beam diffracted by a periodic grating under paraxial approximation, introduce environmental coupling via an effective open-system model that exponentially damps spatial coherences, and analyze both standard observables (intensity, transverse-momentum) and the local probability flow using the Bohmian/hydrodynamic representation.
AI.result: Decoherence progressively suppresses the Talbot carpet and smooths transverse-momentum distributions, but the probability flow can persist as organized channels tied to grating periodicity even after interference fringes vanish. Loss of visible interference and loss of dynamical pathway separation do not necessarily coincide.
AI.conclusion: Flux-channel structures can survive in regimes where multi-slit interference is already strongly reduced, providing a local characterization of decoherence that complements previous trajectory-based analyses.

title: QOuLiPo: What a quantum computer sees when it reads a book
summary:
What does a book look like to a quantum computer? This paper takes eight classical works of the Renaissance and its late-antique inheritance -- from Augustine to Galileo -- and runs each through a neutral-atom quantum processor. The bridge is graphs: each textual unit becomes an atom, and graph edges are physical blockade constraints for engineered exact unit-disk designs, or a 2D approximation to the semantic graph for natural texts.
  Three contributions follow. First, we introduce rigidity rho, a metric for how unique a book's structural backbone is -- distinguishing Marguerite de Navarre's Heptameron (rigid, twelve-nouvelle hard core) from Boethius (fully fungible, every chapter substitutable). Second, we invert the pipeline: rather than extracting a graph from existing prose, we pick a target graph the hardware encodes natively, and write a book whose structure matches it. The twenty-nine texts written this way, collected under the name QOuLiPo, extend the OuLiPo tradition to graph-topological constraints and, together with the eight natural texts, form a benchmark distribution against which neutral-atom hardware can be tracked as it scales. Third, we run both natural and engineered texts on Pasqal's FRESNEL processor up to one hundred atoms; engineered texts reach high approximation ratios, the cleanest instances returning the exact backbone.
  A cloud-accessible quantum machine plus an agentic coding environment now lets a single investigator run this pipeline end-to-end. What is reported is an application layer, not a speedup -- humanistic instances ready to load onto neutral-atom processors as they scale, already complementing classical text analysis. The Digital Humanities community has a stake in building familiarity with this hardware now: the engineered-corpus design choices made today fix the benchmark distribution future hardware will be measured against.

AI.tldr: This paper bridges quantum computing and digital humanities by encoding both classical Renaissance texts and newly written "QOuLiPo" works as graphs on a neutral-atom quantum processor (Pasqal's FRESNEL, up to 100 atoms). It introduces a rigidity metric (ρ) for structural uniqueness, inverts the typical text-to-graph pipeline by writing books to match native hardware graphs, and demonstrates that engineered texts achieve high approximation ratios on quantum hardware, establishing a benchmark distribution for future neutral-atom processors.
AI.motivation: To explore how classical literary texts can be represented and analyzed on quantum hardware, and to establish a benchmark corpus (both natural and engineered) for evaluating neutral-atom quantum processors as they scale, bridging the gap between digital humanities and quantum computing.
AI.method: Eight classical texts (Augustine to Galileo) and twenty-nine engineered "QOuLiPo" texts are converted into unit-disk graphs. Textual units become atoms; graph edges encode physical blockade constraints (exact for engineered designs, approximated 2D semantic graphs for natural texts). The texts are run on Pasqal's FRESNEL neutral-atom quantum processor (up to 100 atoms). A new metric, rigidity (ρ), quantifies structural uniqueness. The pipeline is cloud-accessible with an agentic coding environment for end-to-end execution.
AI.result: The Heptameron is identified as rigid (high ρ, with a hard core of twelve novellas), while Boethius is fully fungible (low ρ). Engineered QOuLiPo texts achieve high approximation ratios on the quantum processor, with the cleanest instances returning exact backbones. The full pipeline operates end-to-end from a single investigator's cloud access.
AI.conclusion: This work establishes an application layer for digital humanities on neutral-atom quantum processors (not a speedup). The engineered-corpus design choices made today will define the benchmark distribution for future hardware. The Digital Humanities community should engage with this hardware now, as current decisions fix the metrics future quantum processors will be evaluated against.

title: Power sensitivity of broadband radiofrequency detectors based on quantum diamond spins
summary: Nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centres in diamond can be used to detect radiofrequency (RF) signals through coupling of the RF magnetic field with the NV spins, combined with optical readout of the spin state. The sensitivity of such RF detectors has so far been mainly studied in terms of magnetic field sensitivity, which is relevant when the RF signal is generated by a near-field source. However, for applications where the RF input is delivered externally, a more relevant quantity is the sensitivity in terms of the input RF power. Here we theoretically analyse the power sensitivity of NV-based RF detectors as a function of the RF-spin interface geometry. We derive scaling laws of the power sensitivity for both slope-detection and variance-detection RF sensing protocols, and for various noise regimes. We find that, in most scenarios, the power sensitivity scales inversely with the characteristic physical dimension of the RF-spin interface, for instance the width of a coplanar waveguide or the diameter of a loop antenna. In other words, the smaller the structure and the probed NV volume, the better the power sensitivity, which is contrary to the case of magnetic field sensitivity. Lastly, we numerically estimate that photon shot noise limited sensitivities of 10^{-20} W Hz^{-1} (slope) and 10^{-12} W Hz^{-1/2} (variance) are achievable. This work lays the groundwork for further optimisation of NV-based RF detectors.

AI.tldr: This paper theoretically analyzes the power sensitivity of NV-based RF detectors, finding that power sensitivity scales inversely with the characteristic physical dimension of the RF-spin interface, and estimates achievable sensitivities of 10^{-20} W Hz^{-1} (slope) and 10^{-12} W Hz^{-1/2} (variance) under photon shot noise limited conditions.
AI.motivation: Previous studies focused on magnetic field sensitivity for NV-based RF detectors, which is relevant for near-field sources, but for externally delivered RF inputs, power sensitivity is more relevant. This work aims to analyze the power sensitivity of NV-based RF detectors.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis of power sensitivity as a function of RF-spin interface geometry, deriving scaling laws for both slope-detection and variance-detection RF sensing protocols across various noise regimes.
AI.result: Power sensitivity scales inversely with the characteristic physical dimension of the RF-spin interface (e.g., waveguide width or loop antenna diameter). Smaller structures and probed NV volumes yield better power sensitivity, contrary to magnetic field sensitivity. Photon shot noise limited sensitivities of 10^{-20} W Hz^{-1} (slope) and 10^{-12} W Hz^{-1/2} (variance) are numerically estimated.
AI.conclusion: This work lays the groundwork for further optimisation of NV-based RF detectors.

title: Worst-Case Sample Complexity Bounds for Distributed Inner Product Estimation with Local Randomized Measurements
summary: We study distributed inner product estimation for $n$-qubit states using local randomized measurements, for which rigorous worst-case guarantees are less understood. We first reduce the minimax kernel optimization to Hamming-distance kernels. Within this class, unbiasedness fixes a unique kernel. For this kernel under local Clifford sampling, we prove a sharp fourth-moment bound using the single-qubit Clifford commutant. This yields worst-case sample complexity $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{4.5^n})$, attained by identical pure product stabilizer states. For the same kernel under local Haar sampling, we prove a local twirling identity that compares its fourth moment with the Clifford fourth moment. This gives the same rigorous upper bound as in the Clifford case, but the comparison is lossy. This motivates the conjectured sharper Haar scaling $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{3.6^n})$ attained by product states, and verify it for several important classes of states. We also show that independent single-qubit Pauli shadows have worst-case scaling $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{7.5^n})$ for large $n$.

AI.tldr: The paper studies worst-case sample complexity of distributed inner product estimation for n-qubit states using local randomized measurements. It finds a unique unbiased kernel via Hamming-distance kernels and shows that under local Clifford sampling, the worst-case complexity is 𝒪(√4.5ⁿ), achieved by identical pure product stabilizer states. Under local Haar sampling, a comparison yields the same bound but a conjectured sharper 𝒪(√3.6ⁿ) is proposed. Independent Pauli shadows scale as 𝒪(√7.5ⁿ).
AI.motivation: To provide rigorous worst-case guarantees for distributed inner product estimation of n-qubit states using local randomized measurements, a regime where such guarantees are not well understood.
AI.method: The authors first reduce minimax kernel optimization to Hamming-distance kernels, where unbiasedness fixes a unique kernel. For this kernel under local Clifford sampling, they prove a sharp fourth-moment bound using the single-qubit Clifford commutant. For local Haar sampling, they prove a local twirling identity comparing its fourth moment to the Clifford fourth moment. Independent single-qubit Pauli shadows are also analyzed.
AI.result: Worst-case sample complexity under local Clifford sampling: 𝒪(√4.5ⁿ). Under local Haar sampling: same rigorous upper bound, but conjectured 𝒪(√3.6ⁿ) (verified for several important state classes). Independent single-qubit Pauli shadows: 𝒪(√7.5ⁿ) for large n.
AI.conclusion: The Clifford bound is tight (attained by identical pure product stabilizer states). The Haar bound may be improvable to √3.6ⁿ, and the Pauli shadow approach is suboptimal. The results provide a rigorous framework for distributed inner product estimation with local measurements.

title: A Qutrit Time Crystal Stabilized with Native Chiral Interactions
summary: Periodically driven quantum many-body systems can spontaneously break discrete time-translation symmetry, realizing discrete time crystals. To date, both experimental and theoretical efforts have largely focused on the simplest case of spontaneous period-doubling in $\mathbb{Z}_2$ discrete time crystals realized with qubits. This owes, in part, to the challenge of stabilizing eigenstate order in higher discrete symmetry ($\mathbb{Z}_n$) time crystals, due to the presence of richer domain wall physics. Here, we demonstrate the realization of a $\mathbb{Z}_3$ discrete time crystal by implementing a Floquet chiral clock model in a chain of 15 superconducting qutrits. Unlike the conventional Ising setting, our system features a tunable chiral angle that governs domain-wall dynamics, spectral degeneracies, and crucially, the stability of time-crystalline order. Using disordered nearest-neighbor chiral interactions, we observe robust subharmonic period tripling that persists across a wide range of drive strengths and is independent of initial state. Finally, we highlight the special role that chirality plays in our $\mathbb{Z}_3$ discrete time crystal -- in its absence, the system's Floquet dynamics exhibit a marked initial state dependence governed by domain wall degeneracies. Our results establish native qudit hardware as a powerful platform to access a broader landscape of non-equilibrium phases.

AI.tldr: The authors realize a $\mathbb{Z}_3$ discrete time crystal using a Floquet chiral clock model in a chain of 15 superconducting qutrits, demonstrating robust subharmonic period tripling stabilized by chirality and disorder, and showing that without chirality the dynamics exhibit strong initial-state dependence.
AI.motivation: Extending discrete time crystals beyond the simplest $\mathbb{Z}_2$ (period-doubling) case to higher symmetry $\mathbb{Z}_n$ time crystals is challenging due to richer domain wall physics; the authors aim to realize and stabilize a $\mathbb{Z}_3$ discrete time crystal.
AI.method: A Floquet chiral clock model is implemented in a chain of 15 superconducting qutrits with tunable chiral angle and disordered nearest-neighbor chiral interactions.
AI.result: Robust subharmonic period tripling is observed across a wide range of drive strengths, independent of initial state. Without chirality, the dynamics show marked initial-state dependence due to domain wall degeneracies.
AI.conclusion: Native qudit hardware is established as a powerful platform for exploring a broader landscape of non-equilibrium phases, and chirality is identified as a crucial ingredient for stabilizing higher-symmetry discrete time crystals.

title: Imaginarity Resource Theory of Gaussian Quantum Channels
summary: Complex numbers play an indispensable role in quantum mechanics and quantum information, as validated by both theoretical analysis and experimental verification. Since quantum information processing inherently relies on quantum channels, the resource theory for quantum channels is equally fundamental to that for quantum states. In this paper, we propose two frameworks for quantifying the imaginarity of Gaussian channels. The first framework regards all real superchannels as free superchannels. Within this setting, we introduce two concrete imaginarity measures for Gaussian channels: I_s^GC based on existing imaginarity measures of Gaussian states, and I_d^GC derived directly from the intrinsic parameters of Gaussian channels, which enjoys high computational simplicity. The second framework adopts only a proper subset of real superchannels as free superchannels. Under this framework, we put forward another imaginarity measure I_c^GC , which is fully determined by the inherent parameters of Gaussian channels and features continuity as well as tractable computation. As a practical application, we employ I_c^GC to investigate the dynamical behavior of Quantum Brownian Motion Gaussian channels throughout the entire evolutionary process.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes two frameworks for quantifying the imaginarity (non-realness) of Gaussian channels in quantum information. The first uses all real superchannels as free operations, introducing two measures (I_s^GC and I_d^GC). The second uses a restricted subset of real superchannels, yielding a measure (I_c^GC) with continuity and computational tractability, applied to Quantum Brownian Motion Gaussian channels.
AI.motivation: Complex numbers are fundamental to quantum mechanics, yet quantifying the imaginarity of quantum channels—as opposed to states—remains underexplored. Since quantum information processing relies on channels, a resource theory for channel imaginarity is needed to parallel that for states.
AI.method: Two frameworks: (1) All real superchannels as free superchannels, yielding measures I_s^GC (via Gaussian state imaginarity) and I_d^GC (directly from channel parameters). (2) A proper subset of real superchannels as free, yielding I_c^GC determined by intrinsic channel parameters, with continuity and computational simplicity.
AI.result: Three imaginarity measures are proposed: I_s^GC, I_d^GC (first framework), and I_c^GC (second framework). I_c^GC is applied to analyze the dynamical behavior of Quantum Brownian Motion Gaussian channels over their entire evolution.
AI.conclusion: The proposed frameworks and measures provide systematic tools for quantifying imaginarity in Gaussian channels, with I_c^GC offering practical advantages for studying channel dynamics, as demonstrated on Quantum Brownian Motion.

title: Quantum optical synthesis of high-dimensional ultrafast frequency-bin qudits
comment: 18 pages and 6 figures. The first two listed authors contributed equally to this work
summary: Frequency modes of light are one of the most promising platforms that provide access to high-dimensional quantum states amongst different photonic degrees of freedom capable of high-dimensionality, enabling robust, error-tolerant, and scalable quantum optical information systems. We demonstrate engineering of precisely controlled two-photon high-dimensional states entangled in frequency through time-domain Fourier optical synthesis. We generate and convert a continuous broadband frequency-entangled state into a large range of discrete frequency bins suitable for ITU standards, with spacings ranging from 12.5 GHz to 750 GHz, and observe spectral anticorrelations over 38 frequency bins, including intra-bin pure states at a 100 GHz bin spacing. We characterize the full quantum state dimensionality via Schmidt decomposition and observe lower bounds on the frequency-binned Hilbert-space dimensionalities of at least 289, formed by two entangled qudits with dimension 17. Furthermore, we demonstrate quantum nonlocality via frequency correlations in a transmission experiment over a campus-scale two-node fiber network. This work represents a crucial step towards building a versatile and relatively simple way of generating precisely controlled high-dimensional spectral qudits, with the potential of harnessing in wavelength-multiplexed quantum networks, high-dimensional information processing, and communication of quantum states specifically, and fiber-optic quantum remote sensing.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates engineering of high-dimensional frequency-entangled two-photon states via time-domain Fourier optical synthesis, achieving spectral anticorrelations over 38 frequency bins, Hilbert-space dimensionality ≥289 (two qudits of dimension 17), and quantum nonlocality over a campus-scale fiber network.
AI.motivation: Frequency modes of light offer a promising platform for high-dimensional quantum states with robustness, error tolerance, and scalability for quantum optical information systems, but precise control over frequency-entangled states remains challenging.
AI.method: Time-domain Fourier optical synthesis is used to generate and convert continuous broadband frequency-entangled states into discrete frequency bins compatible with ITU standards, with spacings from 12.5 GHz to 750 GHz. Full quantum state characterization is performed via Schmidt decomposition.
AI.result: Spectral anticorrelations observed over 38 frequency bins; intra-bin pure states achieved at 100 GHz spacing; lower bound on frequency-binned Hilbert-space dimensionality of at least 289 (two entangled qudits of dimension 17); quantum nonlocality demonstrated in a campus-scale two-node fiber network transmission experiment.
AI.conclusion: This work is a crucial step toward generating precisely controlled high-dimensional spectral qudits with a versatile and simple approach, applicable to wavelength-multiplexed quantum networks, high-dimensional information processing, quantum communication, and fiber-optic quantum remote sensing.

title: Toward Covert Quantum Computing
summary: As quantum computers become available through multi-tenant cloud platforms, ensuring privacy against adversaries sharing the same quantum processing unit becomes critical. We introduce and explore \emph{covert quantum computing}, a new concept that ensures an adversary with access to all other quantum computational units (QCUs) of a quantum computer cannot detect computation on the subset that they cannot access. Analogous to covert communication, we employ information theory. However, since here the adversary controls the systems used for detection, we require a richer framework for covertness analysis that accounts for the use of quantum memories and adaptive operations. Thus, we adopt the \emph{quantum-strategy} framework used in quantum game theory and memory channel discrimination. Current quantum computers use planar graph circuit layouts and typically assume nearest-neighbor crosstalk. We derive discrete isoperimetric inequalities to show that, for an $n$-qubit circuit under this model, only $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{n})$ border qubits provide detection information to the adversary. We then explore this scaling law on IQM's 54-qubit \emph{Emerald} processor and IBM's 156-qubit \emph{ibm\_fez} machine employing the Heron 2 architecture. We implement Ramsey experiments on qubits not used in computation, and detect nearest-neighbor crosstalk, as expected. However, we also observe long-range coupling effects beyond the border qubits, revealing a side channel that the adversary can exploit. We hypothesize that this long-range crosstalk is induced by leakage from the drive and control lines. Beyond weakening covertness, it exposes co-tenants to both adversarial and unintended crosstalk and degrades circuits that span spatially distributed qubits, motivating further work on spatial isolation and crosstalk characterization.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces covert quantum computing, a concept ensuring that computation on a subset of quantum computational units (QCUs) remains undetectable to an adversary with access to all other QCUs in a multi-tenant quantum cloud. Using quantum-strategy frameworks and discrete isoperimetric inequalities, the authors show that only O(√n) border qubits leak detection information in planar nearest-neighbor architectures. Experiments on IQM's 54-qubit Emerald and IBM's 156-qubit ibm_fez processors confirm nearest-neighbor crosstalk but also reveal unexpected long-range coupling, creating a side channel that weakens covertness and poses risks for multi-tenant quantum computing.
AI.motivation: As quantum computing moves to multi-tenant cloud platforms, ensuring privacy against co-located adversaries sharing the same quantum processing unit is critical. Existing privacy models do not account for adversaries with physical access to other parts of the quantum computer, motivating a new framework for covert quantum computing.
AI.method: The authors adopt the quantum-strategy framework from quantum game theory and memory channel discrimination to model the adversary's detection capabilities. They derive discrete isoperimetric inequalities to bound the number of border qubits leaking detection information in planar nearest-neighbor circuit layouts. Experimental validation uses Ramsey measurements on idle qubits to detect crosstalk on IQM's 54-qubit Emerald and IBM's 156-qubit ibm_fez processors.
AI.result: Theoretically, only O(√n) border qubits provide detection information to the adversary. Experiments confirm nearest-neighbor crosstalk but also reveal long-range coupling beyond border qubits, attributed to leakage from drive and control lines, which creates an exploitable side channel.
AI.conclusion: Covert quantum computing is feasible in principle with O(√n) leakage scaling, but current hardware exhibits long-range crosstalk that undermines covertness. This motivates further work on spatial isolation and crosstalk characterization to secure multi-tenant quantum cloud platforms.

title: Stopping Reliability in Adaptive Krylov-Shadow Quantum Fisher Information Estimation
summary: Adaptive quantum Fisher information (QFI) estimation requires a stopping rule that distinguishes accuracy from apparent numerical stability. For Krylov-shadow QFI estimators, finite Krylov order $K$ produces truncation bias, while finite sample budget $M$ produces finite-$M$ sampling-side error. We show that a width-only empirical stopping rule, based on interval width and local Krylov stability, can declare convergence at small $(K,M)$ even when the post hoc error exceeds the requested tolerance; we call this event a \emph{false stop}. The mechanism is a narrow empirical interval centered on a biased low-$K$ estimate. We give a two-component stopping analysis that separates the Krylov and sampling terms, and we implement a guarded rule that permits a success declaration only after minimum thresholds in $K$ and $M$ and a persistence condition are satisfied. On a five-level dephasing benchmark at $n=4$ qubits, the guarded rule suppresses the false success declarations produced by the width-only empirical rule, whose false-stop rates range from $0.16$ to $0.68$ across the tested noise levels. Under the main fixed resource limit, the guarded rule refuses to make success declarations rather than accepting biased low-$K$ estimates; a separate true-relative-tolerance sampling-budget sequence then shows that, after Krylov and sampling recalibration, the same decision principle can make success declarations without observed false stops. These results show that stopping reliability is a distinct design requirement for adaptive QFI estimation: sampling precision at fixed $K$ does not by itself establish that Krylov truncation bias is controlled.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies a "false stop" problem in adaptive quantum Fisher information estimation using Krylov-shadow estimators, where width-only stopping rules can declare convergence prematurely due to biased low-order Krylov estimates. It proposes a guarded stopping rule with minimum thresholds and persistence conditions, demonstrating on a 5-level dephasing benchmark (n=4 qubits) that this rule suppresses false success declarations (false-stop rates 0.16-0.68) and only makes reliable decisions after Krylov and sampling recalibration.
AI.motivation: Adaptive QFI estimation requires reliable stopping rules that distinguish genuine accuracy from apparent numerical stability. Existing width-only empirical rules fail because they can declare convergence at small Krylov order K and sample budget M even when post hoc error exceeds tolerance, due to narrow empirical intervals centered on biased low-K estimates.
AI.method: The authors propose a two-component stopping analysis separating Krylov truncation bias and finite-M sampling error, then implement a guarded stopping rule requiring minimum thresholds in K and M and a persistence condition before a success declaration. They test on a five-level dephasing benchmark at n=4 qubits.
AI.result: The guarded rule suppresses false success declarations produced by the width-only rule (false-stop rates 0.16-0.68 across noise levels). Under fixed resource limits, the guarded rule refuses declarations rather than accepting biased low-K estimates. After Krylov and sampling recalibration, the same principle makes success declarations without observed false stops.
AI.conclusion: Stopping reliability is a distinct design requirement for adaptive QFI estimation; sampling precision at fixed K does not guarantee Krylov truncation bias is controlled.

title: Model Checking Matrix Product States against Linear Chain Logic
summary: Matrix product states (MPS) are a standard tensor-network representation for ground states of one-dimensional quantum many-body systems, and they underpin widely used simulation tools such as DMRG. However, while quantum model checking has been developed mainly for quantum programs and communication protocols (with properties expressed along a time axis), there is still no comparable framework for systematically verifying \emph{spatial} and \emph{size-dependent} properties of physical many-body states, where the key parameter is the system size. This paper takes a step toward bridging the gap. We propose \emph{Linear Chain Logic} (LCL), a spatial logic designed to specify physically meaningful properties of periodic MPS families as the system size grows, such as nontriviality on rings and large-size asymptotic patterns. Our approach builds on a simple but powerful connection: every periodic MPS naturally induces a completely positive map (a quantum operation) on its virtual space, so many quantitative features of the MPS can be analysed through the repeated application of the operation. Using this perspective, we derive an effective procedure to compute the inner products of an MPS at a given size and to support richer LCL specifications, without relying on brute-force state expansion. We then develop approximate model-checking algorithms that combine sound bounding with asymptotic structural analysis, enabling scalable reasoning about large system sizes. Experiments on representative MPS families illustrate that our method can automatically verify nontriviality and detect asymptotic spatial regimes in a way that complements traditional numerical techniques.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Linear Chain Logic (LCL), a spatial logic for verifying properties of periodic matrix product states (MPS) at varying system sizes, leveraging the connection between periodic MPS and completely positive maps to enable efficient model checking without brute-force expansion.
AI.motivation: Quantum model checking has been developed mainly for temporal properties of quantum programs and protocols, but there is no systematic framework for verifying spatial and size-dependent properties of physical many-body states, where system size is the key parameter.
AI.method: The authors propose Linear Chain Logic (LCL) for specifying spatial properties of periodic MPS families. They exploit the fact that every periodic MPS naturally induces a completely positive map on its virtual space, enabling analysis via repeated application of this map. They derive procedures for computing inner products at given sizes and develop approximate model-checking algorithms combining sound bounding with asymptotic structural analysis.
AI.result: The method can automatically verify nontriviality and detect asymptotic spatial regimes in representative MPS families, complementing traditional numerical techniques.
AI.conclusion: The work bridges a gap between quantum model checking and many-body physics by providing a systematic framework for spatial property verification of MPS, scalable to large system sizes without brute-force state expansion.

title: Optimizing the preparation of Dicke states using counterdiabatic driving methods
summary: Recently, the technique of counterdiabatic driving, which provides an effective strategy for accelerating adiabatic quantum evolution, has been widely applied in the preparation of many-body quantum states. In this work, we propose a theoretical scheme for the efficient preparation of Dicke states in a system of non-interacting two-level atoms. Our approach leverages the one-axis twisting (OAT) interaction to generate non-classical correlations and combines it with time-dependent external fields to achieve precise control over the dynamics of the system. By employing rapid adiabatic passage (RAP), it demonstrates how the system can be steered from an initial coherent spin state to a target Dicke state with high fidelity [S. C. Carrasco, M. H. Goerz, S. A. Malinovskaya, V. Vuletić, W. P. Schleich, and V. S. Malinovsky, Phys. Rev. Lett. \textbf{132}, 153603 (2024)]. To further optimize the preparation process, we introduce counterdiabatic driving (CD), which suppresses non-adiabatic transitions. Numerical simulations confirm that our scheme can achieve high-fidelity Dicke states for a moderate number of particles. Our results provide a scalable and experimentally feasible approach to prepare Dicke states, with potential applications in quantum metrology, quantum communication, and quantum information processing.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a scheme to efficiently prepare Dicke states in non-interacting two-level atoms using one-axis twisting (OAT) interaction, rapid adiabatic passage (RAP), and counterdiabatic driving (CD). Numerical simulations confirm high-fidelity preparation for moderate particle numbers, offering a scalable approach for quantum metrology and information processing.
AI.motivation: To develop an efficient and experimentally feasible scheme for preparing Dicke states in non-interacting two-level atomic systems, leveraging counterdiabatic driving to accelerate adiabatic quantum evolution and suppress non-adiabatic transitions.
AI.method: The scheme combines one-axis twisting (OAT) interaction (to generate non-classical correlations) with time-dependent external fields, rapid adiabatic passage (RAP), and counterdiabatic driving (CD) to steer the system from an initial coherent spin state to a target Dicke state with high fidelity.
AI.result: Numerical simulations demonstrate that the proposed scheme can achieve high-fidelity preparation of Dicke states for a moderate number of particles.
AI.conclusion: The approach is scalable and experimentally feasible, with potential applications in quantum metrology, quantum communication, and quantum information processing.

title: Nonreciprocal magnon-magnon entanglement in a spinning cavity-magnon system
summary: Cavity-magnon systems, combining magnons and photons, offer a versatile platform for studying quantum entanglement and advancing quantum information science. In this work, we propose a scheme for generating nonreciprocal magnon-magnon entanglement in a hybrid system consisting of two yttrium iron garnet spheres coupled to a spinning whispering-gallery-mode cavity. By leveraging the magnon Kerr nonlinearity and the Sagnac effect arising from the cavity rotation, we show that the entanglement can be substantially enhanced, and the resulting entanglement exhibits pronounced nonreciprocal characteristics. Furthermore, our scheme demonstrates that the entanglement remains robust against thermal noise and persists at bath temperatures up to 100 mK. This work underscores the potential of spinning cavity-magnon systems as a versatile platform for realizing nonreciprocal quantum devices and facilitating the development of quantum technologies.

AI.tldr: A scheme for generating nonreciprocal magnon-magnon entanglement in a spinning cavity-magnon system using Kerr nonlinearity and Sagnac effect, achieving enhanced, robust entanglement up to 100 mK.
AI.motivation: To generate and enhance nonreciprocal magnon-magnon entanglement in cavity-magnon systems, leveraging the unique properties of spinning cavities and magnon Kerr nonlinearity for quantum information applications.
AI.method: Combines two yttrium iron garnet (YIG) spheres coupled to a spinning whispering-gallery-mode (WGM) cavity; utilizes magnon Kerr nonlinearity and the Sagnac effect from cavity rotation to create nonreciprocal entanglement.
AI.result: Entanglement is substantially enhanced, exhibits pronounced nonreciprocal characteristics, and remains robust against thermal noise up to 100 mK bath temperature.
AI.conclusion: Spinning cavity-magnon systems are a versatile platform for nonreciprocal quantum devices and advancing quantum technologies.

title: Interference visibility as a witness of preparation contextuality via overlap inequalities
summary: We show that standard multi-path interferometry, using only pairwise visibility measurements, provides an operational route to tests of preparation noncontextuality. Under ideal symmetric conditions, interference visibility directly encodes state overlaps, without requiring tomography or SWAP tests. For three paths, any jointly diagonalizable (coherence-free) description must satisfy ${V}_{12}^2+{V}_{23}^2-{V}_{13}^2\le 1$, where ${V}_{ij}$ are two-path visibilities. Pure qubit detector states violate this bound, achieving a maximal value of $5/4$. We generalize to arbitrary $n$-path interferometers and derive the tight qubit bound $S_n^{\max}=n\cos^2(π/2n)-1$ for all $n\ge3$, achieved by coplanar pure qubit states with uniform angular separation $π/n$. A robustness analysis yields explicit experimental thresholds. Under the operational equivalences used in overlap-based generalized noncontextuality frameworks, violations of these visibility inequalities also witness preparation contextuality. For $n$-cycle inequalities, only the pairwise visibilities appearing in the cycle need to be measured.

AI.tldr: Multi-path interferometry with pairwise visibility measurements can test preparation noncontextuality. For three paths, any noncontextual theory satisfies V₁₂²+V₂₃²-V₁₃²≤1, but quantum qubit states violate this bound up to 5/4. Generalized n-path inequalities yield tight qubit bounds S_n^max = n cos²(π/2n)-1, with violations witnessing preparation contextuality.
AI.motivation: To find an operational route to test preparation noncontextuality using standard multi-path interferometry with only pairwise visibility measurements, avoiding the need for full tomography or SWAP tests.
AI.method: Derives visibility inequalities from the assumption of jointly diagonalizable (coherence-free) descriptions. For n-path interferometers, pairwise visibilities are analyzed under ideal symmetric conditions. Coplanar pure qubit states with uniform angular separation π/n are used to derive the maximal quantum violation. Robustness analysis provides experimental thresholds.
AI.result: Three-path noncontextual bound: V₁₂²+V₂₃²-V₁₃²≤1, violated by pure qubit detectors up to 5/4. General n-path tight qubit bound: S_n^max = n cos²(π/2n)-1 for n≥3. Violations witness preparation contextuality under operational equivalences.
AI.conclusion: Multi-path interferometry provides a practical, tomography-free test of preparation noncontextuality via simple visibility inequalities, with explicit experimental thresholds for implementation.

title: Singular Asymptotics of SPADE in Quantum Source Discrimination
summary: We study far-field discrimination between one and two incoherent point sources in the singular regime of weak and closely spaced emitters. Under ideal alignment, spatial-mode demultiplexing (SPADE) attains the quantum-optimal large-sample Stein exponent, but the finite-photon behavior near the one-source boundary and the effect of realistic imperfections remain less understood. Using singular learning theory, we analyze both the aligned and misaligned problems.
